breakfast.name: Beignets de Banane
instructions: Peel and mash the ripe plantains until smooth.
Mix in flour, sugar, vanilla extract, nutmeg, and salt to form a thick batter.
Heat vegetable oil in a deep pan to 350°F.
Drop spoonfuls of batter into the hot oil.
Fry until golden brown on all sides, about 3 to 4 minutes.
Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towels.
Serve warm as a breakfast treat.
breakfast.description: Sweet plantain fritters popular across Gabon, enjoyed as a filling morning snack with coffee or tea.

breakfast.name: Bouillie de Maïs
instructions: Bring the water to a boil in a medium saucepan.
Mix cornmeal with a cup of cold water to form a smooth slurry.
Gradually pour the slurry into the boiling water, stirring constantly.
Reduce heat and cook for 15 minutes, stirring frequently to prevent lumps.
Stir in coconut milk, sugar, vanilla, cinnamon, and salt.
Cook for another 5 minutes until thick and creamy.
Serve warm in bowls.
breakfast.description: A smooth and creamy corn porridge enriched with coconut milk, a staple Gabonese breakfast.

breakfast.name: Beignets de Banane (Banana Fritters)
instructions: Mash bananas, mix with flour, sugar, egg, vanilla, nutmeg
Batter should be thick and spoonable
Drop spoonfuls into hot oil
Fry until golden on all sides — 3-4 min
Drain on paper
The banana sweetness caramelizes in the oil — no additional syrup needed
Serve warm with coffee — Gabon's morning street food
Found at every roadside stall in Libreville by 6am
breakfast.description: Gabon's morning street fritters — ripe banana batter fried golden, naturally sweet. Found at every Libreville roadside stall at dawn. The simplicity and the caramelized banana sweetness make these viral in West-Central African breakfast content.

breakfast.name: Bouillon de Poisson (Morning Fish Broth)
ingredients: Fresh fish (head and bones included — for flavor)
instructions: Simmer fish with tomato, onion, garlic, pepper in palm oil-enriched water
Cook until fish is tender and broth is rich — 15-20 min
The fish head and bones give the broth deep flavor and body
Season with salt and Maggi
Serve as a breakfast soup with boiled plantain on the side
In Gabon, a morning fish broth is as normal as cereal elsewhere
The broth clears the head and starts the day — Gabon's morning fuel
breakfast.description: Gabon's wake-up soup — fresh fish simmered into a rich, palm-oil-enriched broth served with boiled plantain. In Central Africa, soup for breakfast is completely normal and this one starts every fisherman's day.

lunch.name: Nyembwe Chicken
ingredients: Salt and black pepper to taste
instructions: Season chicken pieces with salt, pepper, and garlic.
Heat palm oil in a large pot and brown the chicken on all sides.
Add onions and cook until softened.
Add tomatoes and Scotch bonnet pepper, cook for 5 minutes.
Pour in the palm nut cream and water, stir well.
Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 45 minutes until chicken is tender.
Adjust seasoning and serve with rice or plantains.
lunch.description: Gabon's national dish featuring chicken simmered in rich palm nut sauce, a beloved everyday meal.

lunch.name: Poisson Salé aux Légumes
instructions: Soak the salted fish in water for 2 hours, changing the water twice to remove excess salt.
Boil cassava leaves in salted water for 20 minutes until tender, then drain.
Heat palm oil in a pot and sauté onions and garlic until fragrant.
Add tomatoes and Scotch bonnet pepper, cook until soft.
Flake the fish and add it to the pot.
Stir in the cooked cassava leaves and water.
Simmer for 15 minutes, adjust seasoning, and serve with fufu.
lunch.description: A hearty dish of salt-cured fish cooked with cassava leaves, reflecting Gabon's riverine and coastal food traditions.

lunch.name: Poulet Nyembwe (Chicken in Palm Nut Sauce)
ingredients: Palm nut cream (nyembwe — from palm fruit)
instructions: Brown chicken pieces in oil
Sauté onion, garlic, add tomatoes
Add palm nut cream — this turns the sauce a rich, deep orange
Add Scotch bonnet, smoked fish if using
Simmer 35-40 min until chicken is tender and sauce is thick
The sauce should coat the back of a spoon — rich and glossy
Season with Maggi and salt
Serve with rice or fried plantain
This is Gabon's national dish — every celebration starts with nyembwe
lunch.description: Gabon's national dish — chicken braised in nyembwe (palm nut cream) until the sauce is rich, thick, and deep orange. The palmiest of palm-based stews. Every celebration in Gabon centers on poulet nyembwe. The dramatic orange color and the communal serving make it viral Central African food content.

lunch.name: Smoked Bushmeat Stew
ingredients: Smoked game meat (antelope, porcupine — or substitute smoked pork)
Palm nut cream or peanut butter
instructions: Soak and boil smoked meat until tender
Make sauce with tomatoes, onion, garlic
Add palm nut cream or peanut butter
Add greens
Simmer until thick and rich
The smoke flavor from the meat infuses the entire stew
Serve with boiled or fried plantain
Bushmeat is culturally significant in Gabon — the forest provides
lunch.description: Central African forest cooking — smoked game meat simmered with palm cream and greens. Gabon's dense equatorial forests provide the ingredients for one of Africa's most distinctive culinary traditions. The smokiness and the forest-origin story are part of Gabon's food identity.

lunch.name: Manioc Bâton (Cassava Sticks)
instructions: Soak and ferment peeled cassava for 2-3 days — the fermentation is essential
Mash the fermented cassava into a smooth paste
Wrap tightly in banana leaves into cylinder shapes
Boil or steam for 1 hour until firm
Unwrap — the cassava has become a dense, slightly sour, chewy stick
Slice into rounds
Serve as accompaniment to any stew — it's Central Africa's bread equivalent
The slightly sour, chewy texture is an acquired taste that becomes essential
lunch.description: Fermented cassava wrapped in banana leaves and steamed into dense, chewy sticks — Central Africa's bread. The fermentation gives it a subtle tanginess. Manioc bâton is the starch that anchors every Gabonese meal, and the banana-leaf-wrapped presentation is iconic.

dinner.name: Brochettes de Viande
instructions: Combine peanut oil, soy sauce, lime juice, garlic, ginger, paprika, salt, and pepper in a bowl.
Add beef cubes and marinate for at least 1 hour.
Thread marinated beef, onion, and pepper chunks onto skewers.
Grill over medium-high heat for 10 to 15 minutes, turning frequently.
Baste with remaining marinade while grilling.
Serve hot with a side of attieke or rice.
dinner.description: Grilled beef skewers seasoned with garlic and ginger, a popular evening street food across Gabonese cities.

dinner.name: Manioc Pilé with Smoked Fish Stew
instructions: Boil cassava in salted water until very soft, about 30 minutes.
Drain and pound the cassava in a mortar until smooth and stretchy.
For the stew, heat palm oil and sauté onions and garlic.
Add tomatoes and pepper, cook for 10 minutes.
Flake smoked fish and add to the stew.
Add spinach and water, simmer for 15 minutes.
Serve the pounded cassava alongside the stew.
dinner.description: Pounded cassava served with a smoky fish and vegetable stew, a comforting traditional Gabonese dinner.

dinner.name: Poisson Braisé (Charcoal-Grilled Fish)
ingredients: 2 whole fresh fish (sea bream, barracuda, or captain fish)
Marinade: lemon juice, garlic, ginger, Scotch bonnet, onion, parsley
Fried plantain and bobolo (cassava stick) for serving
instructions: Score fish deeply on both sides
Make marinade paste: blend garlic, ginger, Scotch bonnet, onion, parsley
Rub paste into fish, inside and out
Grill over charcoal until skin is charred and crispy, flesh is flaky
Baste with palm oil during grilling for color and flavor
Serve with fried plantain and bobolo
The charcoal smoke and the Scotch bonnet marinade create an intense flavor
Roadside poisson braisé stands are Libreville's night food scene
dinner.description: Gabon's charcoal-grilled whole fish — marinated in a fiery Scotch bonnet paste and basted with palm oil over charcoal. The roadside poisson braisé stands along Libreville's streets at night are viral Central African food content — smoke, flame, and the charred skin reveal.

dinner.name: Chocolat Indigène (Gabonese Hot Chocolate)
ingredients: Cacao beans (roasted, ground — Gabon grows cacao)
instructions: Roast raw cacao beans until fragrant
Grind into a paste — this is the chocolate base
Dissolve cacao paste in hot milk or water
Add sugar, vanilla, cinnamon
Simmer until thick and rich
Serve hot — this is chocolate from the source
Gabon produces cacao — this drink connects directly to the tree
The 'bean-to-cup' story is a powerful one in a cacao-growing country
dinner.description: Hot chocolate made from locally grown cacao beans — Gabon produces cacao, making this a true bean-to-cup experience. The origin story and the simplicity of the preparation (roast, grind, boil) have gained attention in the single-origin chocolate movement.

snacks.name: Chin-Chin
instructions: Mix flour, sugar, baking powder, nutmeg, and salt in a bowl.
Add butter, egg, and milk, then knead into a smooth dough.
Roll the dough out to 1/4-inch thickness on a floured surface.
Cut into small strips or squares.
Heat oil to 350°F and fry the pieces in batches until golden brown.
Drain on paper towels and let cool.
Store in an airtight container.
snacks.description: Crispy fried dough bites flavored with nutmeg, a crunchy snack enjoyed across Central Africa.

snacks.name: Beignets de Manioc (Cassava Fritters)
instructions: Mix fermented cassava dough with sugar, vanilla or nutmeg
Shape into balls or flat rounds
Deep fry until golden — 3-4 min
The fermentation adds a slight tanginess to the sweet fritter
Drain and serve warm
Found everywhere in Gabon — the cheapest, most satisfying snack
The tangy-sweet contrast from the fermented cassava is unique
snacks.description: Fermented cassava fritters — slightly tangy from the fermentation, slightly sweet from the sugar. Gabon's cheapest and most ubiquitous street snack.

snacks.name: Ndolé (Bitter Leaf and Peanut Stew)
ingredients: Bitter leaves (ndolé leaves) — or substitute spinach/kale
instructions: Wash bitter leaves multiple times to reduce bitterness — this takes patience
Boil leaves, drain, squeeze out water — repeat 2-3 times
Ground peanuts into a paste
Sauté onion, garlic in palm oil
Add peanut paste, dried shrimp, smoked fish
Add the prepared bitter leaves
Simmer 30 min until thick and unified
The bitterness of the leaves balanced by the richness of the peanuts is the magic
Season with Maggi and salt
snacks.description: Bitter leaf stew with ground peanuts and dried shrimp — a Cameroonian-origin dish deeply loved across Central Africa including Gabon. The bitter-rich contrast and the patient leaf-washing process (boil, squeeze, repeat) have made ndolé viral as West-Central Africa's most complex green stew.

snacks.name: Beignets de Banane Plantain (Plantain Fritters)
instructions: Mash very ripe plantains until smooth
Mix with flour, sugar, nutmeg — batter should be thick
Drop spoonfuls into hot oil
Fry until deep golden — 3-4 min
Drain briefly
The natural sweetness of the plantain means less added sugar needed
These are Gabon's afternoon snack — served with coffee or tea
The plantain gives a unique flavor that wheat-only beignets can't match
snacks.description: Gabon's plantain beignets — mashed ripe plantain in the batter creates fritters with natural sweetness and a flavor that plain wheat beignets can't touch. The Francophone African fritter tradition with a tropical twist.

desserts.name: Gâteau de Manioc
instructions: Preheat oven to 350°F and grease a baking pan.
Squeeze excess moisture from grated cassava.
Mix cassava with coconut milk, sugar, eggs, melted butter, vanilla, cinnamon, and salt.
Pour the mixture into the prepared pan and smooth the top.
Bake for 40 to 45 minutes until golden and set.
Let cool for 10 minutes before slicing.
Serve warm or at room temperature.
desserts.description: A moist cassava cake baked with coconut milk and warm spices, a beloved Gabonese dessert.

desserts.name: Gâteau de Patate (Sweet Potato Cake)
instructions: Boil and mash sweet potato
Mix with sugar, eggs, flour, vanilla, spices, melted butter
Pour into greased baking dish
Bake at 175°C for 35-40 min until set and golden on top
The natural sweetness of the sweet potato means less added sugar is needed
Let cool slightly — serve warm or at room temperature
Dense, moist, and aromatic — like a tropical pumpkin pie but with sweet potato
desserts.description: Gabonese sweet potato cake — dense, moist, and naturally sweet from the potato. A Central African dessert that needs minimal added sugar. The tropical warmth of cinnamon, nutmeg, and vanilla make this a comforting, shareable dessert.

desserts.name: Bananes Flambées (Flambéed Bananas)
instructions: Melt butter in a pan, add brown sugar — let it caramelize
Add halved bananas, cook until golden — 2 min per side
Add rum — carefully flambé (tip pan toward flame or use a lighter)
The flames burn off the alcohol leaving rum flavor behind
Sprinkle cinnamon
Serve over vanilla ice cream
The flambé technique is the dramatic moment
Gabon's French colonial influence shows in desserts like this
desserts.description: Flambéed bananas in rum and brown sugar — Gabon's French colonial dessert heritage meets tropical fruit. The dramatic flame moment when the rum catches fire is the viral hook, and the caramelized banana over ice cream is pure indulgence.

desserts.name: Gâteau de Manioc (Cassava Cake)
instructions: Grate cassava and coconut finely
Mix with sugar, eggs, melted butter, vanilla, cinnamon
Pour into a greased baking pan
Bake at 175°C for 35-40 min until golden and firm
The cassava gives a unique, slightly chewy texture — denser than wheat cake
The coconut adds moisture and tropical flavor
Let cool slightly — the texture improves as it sets
Serve warm or at room temperature — equally good both ways
This is Gabon's contribution to the Central African cassava-cake tradition
desserts.description: Gabon's cassava cake — grated cassava and coconut baked into a dense, chewy, naturally sweet cake. The cassava texture (unlike any wheat flour cake) and the coconut richness make this a uniquely Central African dessert.

drinks.name: Jus de Gingembre
instructions: Blend ginger with 2 cups of water until smooth.
Strain through a fine sieve or cheesecloth into a pitcher.
Add remaining water, sugar, lemon juice, and vanilla.
Stir until sugar dissolves completely.
Refrigerate until well chilled.
Serve over ice with fresh mint leaves.
drinks.description: A refreshing and spicy ginger juice popular throughout Gabon, served cold as a thirst quencher.

drinks.name: Vin de Palme
instructions: Collect fresh palm sap from a tapped palm tree early in the morning.
Strain the sap through a clean cloth to remove any debris.
Allow the sap to ferment naturally for 6 to 12 hours for a mildly alcoholic drink.
Serve chilled over ice with lime wedges.
Consume within 24 hours as it continues to ferment and sour.
drinks.description: Naturally fermented palm wine, a traditional alcoholic beverage tapped fresh from palm trees in Gabon.

drinks.name: Jus de Gingembre (Ginger Juice)
instructions: Peel and blend ginger with water
Strain through cloth — squeeze out all the juice
Add sugar or honey to taste
Add lime juice and optional pineapple juice
Chill thoroughly
Serve over ice — the ginger burn should be noticeable but not painful
Adjust sweetness and lime to balance the ginger heat
Every Central and West African market has a ginger juice vendor
drinks.description: Fresh ginger juice — fiery, refreshing, and sold at every market in Central Africa. The ginger burn balanced by lime and sweetness is addictive. Viral as a natural energy drink and cold remedy across West and Central Africa.

drinks.name: Jus de Corossol (Soursop Juice)
instructions: Peel soursop, remove seeds — the flesh is white and fibrous
Blend flesh with water or milk
Strain if desired — some like it pulpy
Add sugar, vanilla, lime juice
Chill — serve ice cold
The flavor is unique — creamy, tangy, tropical, like strawberry-pineapple-coconut
Soursop grows abundantly in Gabon's tropical climate
The juice is thick, almost milkshake-like when made with milk
Soursop is having a global moment for its reported health benefits
drinks.description: Gabon's soursop juice — the creamy, tangy, tropical fruit blended into a thick shake that tastes like strawberry-pineapple-coconut had a baby. Soursop grows abundantly in Gabon's equatorial climate and is having a global viral moment for its health claims.

drinks.name: Vin de Palme (Palm Wine)
ingredients: Palm tree sap (tapped from oil palm or raffia palm)
instructions: A tapper climbs the palm tree — a skilled, dangerous job
Cuts into the tree's crown to collect the sap in a calabash or container
The sap flows for hours — sweet and milky when fresh (called 'sweet toddy')
Left to sit, wild yeasts ferment it naturally — within hours it becomes mildly alcoholic
By day 2-3 it's stronger and more sour
By day 4+ it becomes palm vinegar
The window for 'perfect' palm wine is narrow — day 1-2
Fresh palm wine is sweet, slightly fizzy, milky white, mildly alcoholic
This is Central Africa's oldest drink — the palm trees are the brewery
In Gabon, palm wine is ceremonial, social, and daily
drinks.description: Gabon's palm wine — sap tapped directly from palm trees, naturally fermented by wild yeasts within hours into a mildly alcoholic, milky, slightly fizzy drink. The tree-climbing tapper, the narrow 'perfect window,' and the spontaneous fermentation make palm wine one of the world's most viral fermentation stories.
